How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models
abstract: Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA) , an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models. Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads ranking models. This post walks through this process that we call “technique propagation” and how we’re optimizing the process using AI agents. Since agents began driving execution in March 2026, we estimate AI agents handle over 60% of all technique propagation. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show 3x greater engineering productivity, a median 4x reduction in training compute across select combinations, and an estimated $45M+ in compute savings by the end of the year. Meta’s ads recommendation system is powered by a large number of distinct ads ranking models, each serving different product surfaces and advertiser objectives, and each with its own architecture, training data, and serving constraints. Across this portfolio, ML researchers and engineers are continuously advancing the state-of-the-art through innovations we call “techniques.” A technique is anything that makes a ranking model better such as architectural advancements like Wukong factorization layers, Interformer interaction networks, richer data representations, training optimizations, or efficiency improvements in training and inference. However, because each model has its own architecture, data, and training and serving constraints, a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next. At the same time, speed matters because ML techniques have a shelf life. An innovation that delivers gains today may be superseded within a couple of model development cycles. The faster proven techniques reach the full model fleet, the more value they deliver before the next generation of techniques arrive. So how do we propagate a technique to a diverse fleet of models as quickly as possible, while minimizing engineering bandwidth and compute? Scaling Technique Propagation Propagating a growing inventory of proven techniques across a large fleet of diverse models creates a combinatorially expanding space of technique-model combinations to explore, where both engineering bandwidth and compute become significant constraints. The standard way to adapt a technique is to have engineers who are domain experts manually execute adaptation. An engineer studies how a technique interacts with a specific model’s architecture, generalizes it, and tunes it to that model’s constraints. This produces the strongest results, and is still the process for our highest-revenue models, but it does not scale to all of the models in the space. Each adaptation is effort-intensive and demands deep familiarity with both the technique and the target model. So throughput is capped by engineering bandwidth while the opportunity for adaptation grows much faster. The second constraint on propagation is compute. Every adaptation attempt requires a training run, and with a finite compute budget the question is not only which techniques to try but how to navigate the combinatorial space of configurations without spending the budget on attempts (most of which will produce suboptimal gains). Both constraints point to the same requirement: To propagate techniques to a large number of diverse models quickly, propagation has to become standardized, automated, and able to make judgment calls. We started by standardizing model design and automating propagation: a template-driven approach organizes models into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, so a technique validated once at the template level propagates automatically to every model built from that template. title: Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Building a Template-Driven ML Ecosystem
abstract: As ML ecosystems grow to a large number of production models, the bottleneck is no longer inventing new techniques to improve these models, but rather shipping them reliably and efficiently across a fragmented model space, creating a rising tide that lifts all the boats. At Meta, we built a template-driven approach that standardizes model design into a small set of reusable and composable building blocks, turning model iteration from a per-model problem into a shared systems problem. Over the last two years, this approach reduced per-model engineering time by 92%, shipped 5000+ technique-model combinations, improved offline model quality by 0.63% on average at neutral serving capacity, and delivered 0.86% cumulative online lift covering 70% of models by count. This work is fully detailed in our paper, “ Design Once, Deploy at Scale: Template-Driven ML Development for Large Model Ecosystems .” Meta’s ads ranking systems process billions of daily requests across a diverse array of products and optimization goals, served by a large number of production models. At that scale, the main challenge in improving user relevance and advertiser value has shifted from inventing new techniques to propagating them. Every high-impact idea needs to reach every model it applies to, and adapting it one model at a time does not scale with the fleet. Fragmentation compounds quickly in large-scale ML systems. A new architecture lands on one model, but bringing it to every corner of the ecosystem may take years. A platform migration works for one family of models, but breaks on a long tail of specialized configurations. A tuning insight improves one model, but says little about the next one because the underlying setup is too different. Over time, propagation becomes more difficult than the innovation itself. Meta’s ads ranking ecosystem ran into this exact problem. As the number of production models grew with the diversity of ads optimization objectives, so did the diversity of architectures, features, training settings, serving constraints, and platform-specific logic. That diversity gave teams flexibility, but it also created three systemic problems: high engineering cost to ship new ideas broadly, high reliability cost from an explosion of corner cases, and low predictability when trying to estimate the ecosystem-wide impact of a change. The deeper issue is that fragmentation creates an unfavorable scaling law for engineering itself. If each idea must be evaluated and adapted per model, the work grows linearly with the number of models. That is manageable early on, but becomes a serious bottleneck when you have a large number of models. Fragmentation also weakens automation. AutoML and optimization systems work best in a structured space, but when every model has a different shape, the highest-potential techniques reach only a subset of models. Our answer was not to add another layer of automation on top of this complexity. Instead, we started by reducing the complexity itself. We did this by introducing Standard Model Templates (SMT), an approach that standardizes model design into a curated set of reusable templates. Figure 1: Before SMT, each technique was tuned by hand on each model, and the combinations to try grew exponentially. With SMT, multi-model optimization tunes techniques once across representative models, and the ones that generalize go into the next template version. A Template-Driven Foundation A template is an opinionated, minimal model setup built from shared components such as architecture choices, feature logic, training settings, and serving configs. Instead of maintaining every production model as a largely independent design, we group similar models around a smaller number of standard templates. Model-specific logic still exists where necessary, but the common parts are explicitly represented and shared. title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
abstract: Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first? Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential. This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come. title: Mathematical proof, powered by AI. And no hallucinations!
abstract: Every day brings new evidence of the awesome power of AI. There have been dramatic developments in mathematics: AI models are solving tough problems from Mathematical Olympiads and even some big open research problems. But AI agents are notorious for simply making stuff up, or “hallucinating”: don’t we have to check their solutions carefully? In fact, the computer can check the agent’s proofs for us, and better still, proof checking can be interleaved with proof generation, keeping it on the right track. To be checked, the proof must be written in some logical formalism: a precise language that expresses mathematical reasoning. Proof assistants are apps designed for writing and checking formal proofs. They include Lean, favored by many mathematicians; HOL Light, used at AWS to formally verify high-performance cryptographic code (including for post-quantum cryptography); and Isabelle, used at AWS to verify the Nitro Isolation Engine. They were originally built to help human users write proofs, but now the “user” will be an AI agent. Most proof assistants are suitable for this task. In this post, we’ll focus on Isabelle. To generate formal proofs, we need a way for the AI agent and the proof assistant to talk to each other. Fortunately, we have the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which is supported by all the leading AI agents. Conceptually, the MCP is a wire connecting an agent to a tool (here, a proof assistant), which may need to be modified to accept the connection. Some proof assistants, like HOL Light, provide a simple command-line interface, sometimes called a REPL (for read-eval-print loop): the user types commands, and HOL Light replies. Connecting an agent to a REPL is easy. But most proof assistants provide sophisticated user interfaces, such as the Lean extension for Microsoft VS Code. That’s great for human users, but an AI agent needs something simple and direct. So we are proud to announce the following tools, which are publicly available in the AutoCorrode verification suite: I/Q: This enables an AI agent to communicate with a live Isabelle session running on your computers. It allows you to temporarily hand over control of the proof assistant to the AI to fill in some formal material or to assess the context and provide advice. I/R: This enables an agent to develop proofs or other formal material while the user keeps working with the proof assistant. The agent still “talks” directly to the proof assistant to know if its proofs work, but it does not take control the way I/Q does. Isabelle Assistant: Powered by I/Q, this provides an Isabelle user with a chat window to an AI agent, which can observe and modify the user’s session, developing or fixing proofs. It’s less powerful than the full I/Q and I/R package but runs in a convenient window, right out of the box. To get an idea of how effective AI is at solving mathematical problems, let’s look at some well-known examples, done automatically with the help of Isabelle Assistant. The square root of two is irrational The ancient Greeks were already aware that the square root of two could not be written as a fraction. Suppose that √2 = a/b is a fraction in lowest terms. Then 2b2 = a2, implying that a is even. But then a = 2k for some k. Then 2b2 = 4k2, so b2 = 2k2 and now b is even. But in that case, a/b is not a fraction in lowest terms. From this contradiction, we conclude that no such fraction exists. Here is the same proof, formalized for Isabelle by Claude Opus 4.6: As with all proof assistants, the language is designed to be checkable by computer. But it is also designed to be human-readable. Here is a little guide: assume introduces an assumption have and show claim some formula to be true obtain claims that certain values exist by gives the justification of a claim We use show when proving facts that we are committed to proving and have when proving facts that we need along the way. title: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 launches in review, part 2
abstract: Once a model is in production, the questions change. Teams want to know which configuration the model should run on now that traffic is real, how to fit more models onto GPUs they already pay for, what to do when the next model is too large for one machine, why requests wait in one Region while GPUs sit idle in another, and why latency rose when nobody changed anything. This post takes those questions in the order teams usually meet them. For HyperPod Inference, it listed additional routing strategies, broader support for model serving frameworks, and expanded multi-Region networking. The Inference Gateway delivers the routing, and managed NVIDIA Dynamo is a new serving framework. For managed endpoints, the roadmap pointed to deeper integration with the rest of the AWS AI landscape. Inference recommendations now run from Amazon SageMaker AI Studio, the SageMaker Python SDK, and the coding agents engineers already use, and endpoints can now route requests across Regions and accounts. To keep each section concrete, we follow one hypothetical team through the blog post. In the spring, they launched a customer support assistant on a 70B-parameter model behind a single SageMaker AI endpoint, using the launches from part 1. By the fall, they need to support more product lines, adopt a larger reasoning model, serve customers in a second Region, and keep their GPU bill flat. The launches at a glance Figure 1: The five stages in this post and the launches in each Choose the right configuration from wherever you work The team picked its first configuration from a benchmark run in April. Since then, they have added four LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters, one for each product line, and the product team has set a target of 500 milliseconds for time to first token (TTFT) at peak load. The April configuration was never tested against either change. The engineers who will re-run the analysis work in notebooks and coding agents, and few of them use the console. Inference recommendations launched in April as an API. Four updates since then make it available in more of the places teams work, and let it answer two harder questions: how many adapters an endpoint can carry, and how much concurrency it can take before it misses a latency target. A new agent skill brings the same expertise into coding agents. Inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Studio (July 2026) Blog: Launching UI for generative AI inference recommendations in Amazon SageMaker AI The April launch automated instance, container, and optimization selection through APIs. Inference recommendations are now also available in SageMaker AI Studio as a guided, low-code workflow. In Studio, choose Jobs , then Inference optimization . Choose a use-case profile (Interact, Generate, Summarize, or Custom), an optimization goal (minimize latency, maximize throughput, or minimize cost), and a model from SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the Model Registry, or an existing SageMaker model. SageMaker AI benchmarks candidate configurations on real GPU infrastructure using NVIDIA AIPerf and applies techniques that match the goal, such as speculative decoding for throughput or kernel tuning for latency. You compare the ranked results by TTFT, inter-token latency, throughput, and cost, and then deploy the chosen configuration to a real-time endpoint from Studio. Inference recommendations in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (August 2026) Blog: LLM optimization integration for Amazon SageMaker Python SDK Benchmarking and recommendations previously required SageMaker AI Studio or direct Boto3 calls. They are now part of the SageMaker Python SDK v3 (version 3.17.0 and later), the same interface teams use for training and deployment, so the workflow fits into notebooks, CI pipelines, and MLOps workflows. You can benchmark a live endpoint against your workload traffic, generate ranked recommendations for a latency, throughput, or cost goal, and deploy the top-ranked configuration

title: Use Kimi Code CLI with models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi Code CLI is an open source coding agent from Moonshot AI, the creator of the Kimi series of open-weight foundation models. Previously, using Kimi Code with models on Amazon Bedrock meant configuring a generic connection “provider” with an Amazon Bedrock API key. For many AWS customers, this meant introducing an extra credential to obtain and protect. With v2.7.0, Moonshot AI adds a native bedrock provider to the CLI. You can now configure the agent to use your standard AWS credential chain, including named profiles and single sign-on (SSO), instead of creating and managing a separate API key. In this post, we show you how to connect Kimi Code CLI to models on Amazon Bedrock using your existing AWS credentials. We use Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed as an example, which supports streaming, configurable reasoning, image input, and client-side tool calling. What’s new Amazon Bedrock provides pay-per-token inference for a range of open and proprietary models from leading providers, available through standard APIs . Processing stays within the AWS data boundary, as detailed in the Data protection section of the User Guide. The model cards detail which APIs and features are supported for each model. In older versions of the Kimi Code CLI, you could connect to Amazon Bedrock through a provider with type = "openai" or type = "openai_responses" . These use the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions or Responses APIs, respectively. This approach required you to set the regional base_url and provide an Amazon Bedrock API key . The key could be short-term or long-term, but it was a separate credential for you to obtain and manage. The native provider changes that setup: Use your existing AWS authentication workflow. The bedrock provider can resolve temporary credentials through the standard AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) credential chain. You can use the default chain or select a named profile, including a profile backed by SSO. Override the protocol for each model, if needed. The provider infers an API format and regional endpoint from the model ID, but you can change them as detailed in the “Override endpoint URL and protocol” section of this post. AWS recommends short-term credentials over long-term credentials. This new path reduces reliance on manually managed API keys, but it doesn’t change your responsibility to protect AWS credentials and scope permissions appropriately. How it works The native provider handles authentication and request routing in four steps: Resolve AWS credentials. Unless you configure an Amazon Bedrock API key, the bedrock provider uses the standard AWS credential chain in your environment. You can set AWS_PROFILE to select a specific named profile . Generate a short-lived bearer token. The provider uses @aws/bedrock-token-generator to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, and renews it when necessary. You don’t need to place any AWS access key or manually generated Amazon Bedrock key in the Kimi Code config.toml . However, an explicit key given through api_key or api_key_env takes precedence if you provide it. Build the regional endpoint. The provider resolves AWS_REGION or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION and constructs the appropriate bedrock-runtime endpoint for the model’s inferred API. For Kimi models, this resolves to the recommended OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions path. Call the selected inference profile. The model alias maps to an Amazon Bedrock model or inference profile ID. This example uses the global inference profile global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 . The global. prefix selects the profile, while AWS_REGION determines the regional endpoint that receives your request. The CLI then streams the model response and can use the model’s client-side tool-calling support during coding tasks. Authentication, authorization, model access, and network connectivity must all succeed for a request to complete. The ephemeral API keys generated by the provider are valid for up to 12 hours or your AWS session length, whichev

title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
abstract: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace , so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer . Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily What’s launching today Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill. To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID. An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace , agents can only buy the products it allows. In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account. title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
abstract: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Solution Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity. Govern proactively, not retroactively Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance: Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations. Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels: Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop): Every action requires explicit human approval. This is the starting point for new agents and high-risk operations. Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop): The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review. Suitable for medium-risk tasks with defined inputs, outputs, and rollback options. Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails): The agent operates independently within strictly defined policy boundaries, enforced deterministically rather than through prompt instructions (see below). title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
abstract: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it. AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace. At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use. Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer. 1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust. Quick knows your business, not only your prompts Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it. Quick does not stop at your Amazon store A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone. It turns data into decisions you can act on Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it. Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays. The Amazon Selling Partner plugin The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
abstract: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result. In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring. Solution overview SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action. Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost. Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step. Recommend (opt in) – One selection opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker Studio, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic, so you can benchmark alternatives on separate compute. title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
abstract: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create q uestions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently . Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-le d, structured interviewing. Three core design principles 1. Build interviews around job-related evidence Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover. The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience. 2. Separate interviewing from scoring Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passa ges. The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. 3. Build fairness protections into the design Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information. What the research shows To understand how well the se design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency. Connect Talent keeps interview questions focused on job-relevant skills The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
abstract: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands capabilities, on AWS Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. A more capable managed harness Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence. Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior. Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost. Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses . Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context

title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
abstract: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access. With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details. Hear it for yourself Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded. From recordings to TTS voice. A few minutes of our science lead Trevor’s source audio, and the resulting generative voice. Recorded: “Hello, I’m Trevor, from Science.” Cloned voice: “That first sentence was my real voice. This is my cloned voice, created from a few minutes of my recordings. It can read any text you give it.” Supports seven languages. Hear Jonas, one of the authors, speaking German in his recording and then in his cloned voice: Recorded: “Hallo, ich bin Jonas. Das ist meine echte Stimme.” (Hi, I’m Jonas. This is my real voice.) Cloned voice: “Und das ist meine geklonte Stimme! Gleiche Stimme, neue Worte: Diesen Satz habe ich geschrieben, aber nie aufgenommen.” (And this is my cloned voice! Same voice, new words: I wrote this sentence, but never recorded it.) Use in a variety of applications. Here’s Trevor in a new job he hasn’t had: a non-player character in a game. “Who’s that crossing my bridge? Oh, it’s you again. Same deal as last time: answer my riddle, or hand over the sandwich.” Expand your voice library with voice cloning. Hear this audio sample from AWS Chief Evangelist Jeff Barr: a real recording, then his cloned voice. Recorded: “Hi, I’m Jeff, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “And this is how my cloned voice sounds, reading a sentence I never recorded.” Hannah: a real recording, then her cloned voice on a support line. Recorded: “Hello, I’m Hannah. This is my real voice.” Cloned voice: “Thanks for calling AnyCompany. Your order 4471 9902 ships today and should arrive on Thursday between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.” Joely: a real recording, then her cloned voice narrating a lesson. Recorded: “Hi, I’m Joely, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “In this module, we’ll look at how a neural network learns. First, it makes a guess. Then it measures how far off that guess was, and adjusts, a little at a time.” What you can build A consistent brand voice across channels Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel. Contact centers Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before roll

title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
abstract: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The six optimization levers The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
abstract: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale. Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI , and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League. What is AWS AI League? AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps: Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge. Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission. Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale. Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges: Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Lambda Event Functions . Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents. Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition. Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency. Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025 Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus The Cisco and AWS partnership The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including: Cisco SD-WAN , whose controller architecture runs on AWS and serves customers globally as a software as a service (SaaS) application. Cisco Meraki , Cisco Spaces , and Cisco’s IoT and smart buildings group. Cisco Cloud Control , a cloud-native, AI-powered application integrated with AWS services that brings together security, networking, observability, and collaboration. Cisco AI Defense , where Cisco’s security team uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker

title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI . When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably. Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does. You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why. A few terms describe the pieces: Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes. Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model . A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others. Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only. Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy. Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why. The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region. Figure 1: Each request

title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant. Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context. The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details. With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. The merchant results come back the same, the provider never learns who the cust

title: PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time. As an AWS customer, you can subscribe to Dialog-RSN-1 through AWS Marketplace and deploy it as a SageMaker endpoint inside your own AWS environment. You can also deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker Studio following the steps in Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . That means the model designed to handle your customer conversations can be deployed like other Amazon SageMaker models with an AWS Marketplace subscription. Deploying Dialog-RSN-1 inside AWS Dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace . It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving. All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place. You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today. To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace , then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements. Built for speed and accuracy Models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff. With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak. Real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond. A model that hears calls the way humans do Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate m

title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
abstract: GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) . Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation. NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator . KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment. Choose a GPU sharing approach MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs . Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG , time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin , and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter . For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA. GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization
abstract: Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a company’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge. Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) , so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI. Full Fine-Tuning: Why it matters Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inherently limits the representation power of the fine-tuned model. As tasks grow more complex and datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples, LoRA hits an accuracy plateau where increasing rank (and thus trainable parameters) fails to bridge the accuracy gap with standard fine-tuning. This plateau reveals that the performance gap isn’t simply because of fewer parameters. It’s caused by rank deficiency itself. The low-rank update can’t capture the full complexity of the weight changes needed for deep task adaptation. However, for complex tasks and domains where large, good-quality datasets exist, full-rank fine-tuning excels by updating model parameters simultaneously. FFT modifies the model’s weight matrix uniformly, using the full representational capacity of the model’s weight matrices rather than restricting updates to a small subspace, and without introducing the abrupt, localized distortions characteristic of low-rank methods. The result is stronger model convergence, better activation alignment across model layers, and a model that faithfully captures both the target task distribution and the richness of its pre-trained knowledge. FFT’s quality advantage grows with dataset scale: at 100K+ training examples, FFT achieved 90.0 percent on LLM-as-Judge semantic correctness across code generation tasks, as shown in the following chart.
