title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips
abstract: At Exa , we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware ( AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2 ), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization. Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving. Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database. Embedding documents at scale Our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices. Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill The preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the new model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices. Optimization journey AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance ( inf2.xlarge ), with one chip and two NeuronCores . Our workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so we run Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving us container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. The same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Our initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model. From that baseline, it became a march to push throughput (docs/sec) as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. The following chart shows the throughput gains at each milestone. Figure 3: Throughput improvement across optimization milestones Starting from the naive compile, a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement. The first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. We also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. The downcast outputs met our correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference (see Agentic methodology ), so the accuracy impact was within our acceptance threshold. title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads. SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working. In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem: MultiNodeTrainingValidation is a new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs. Hung job detection finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it. Why node health alone isn’t enough The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them: Numerical faults – A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run. Meta attributed 6 of the 419 unexpected interruptions in its 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run to silent data corruption ( The Llama 3 Herd of Models ). Hung jobs – An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log. Cluster-level failures – Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. HMA checks each node on its own, so it doesn’t see these problems. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it. Solution overview Each capability c

title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
abstract: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case. Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard , a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model. What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard? The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information: Quality scores on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable. Performance and cost metrics that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run. Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model. Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio Key concepts This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves. Quality benchmarks A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs: Benchmark What it measures, in plain terms BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic. GPQA Diamond Graduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning. MMLU-Pro Broad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions. Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark. Use case profiles and optimization goals Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see: Use case profile. Select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu. The default is Max Context. The profile changes only the performance and cost metrics. Quality benchmark scores are the same for every profile. Optimization goal. title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS. As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks. In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models. Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task. After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why. Solution overview You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch: Latency: InvocationLatency , TimeToFirstToken , OutputTokenCount , and output tokens per second (OTPS), which you derive. Throttling: InvocationThrottles , plus the tokens each request reserves against your quota, which you publish yourself. Bedrock also publishes EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage , which measures your estimated tokens per minute (TPM) quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across all inference APIs ( Converse , InvokeModel , ConverseStream , and InvokeModelWithResponseStream ). You can use this metric to set proactive alarms before reaching your quota limit, track your quota consumption across your models, and request further quota increases before usage is rate limited. Cost: InputTokenCount (uncached input), CacheReadInputTokenCount , CacheWriteInputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount , each priced at its own rate. Cache reads cost less than uncached input, and cache writes can cost more depending on the model. A lower cache hit rate can increase cost per request. On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model. Architecture Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock. title: Engineering AI Discover
abstract: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan , Peng Ren , Gary Tang , Itay Teller , Atif Faheem , Nipun Kumar , Donnie DeBoer , Eduardo Lundgren , Matteo Rinaldi , Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover , a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way. Why an intelligence layer? Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer. The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design: Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. title: De-identifying text at scale: How Airbnb protects personal data in AI training
abstract: Here’s how Airbnb detects and replaces personal data in messages, reviews, and support chats before it reaches a model. By: Emelin Flores , Alex Klimov , Lee Formyduval , Bahador Nooraei Introduction Airbnb is built on trust. Every night that a guest books a stay, or a host welcomes someone into their home, that trust is backed by information they’ve shared with us, which includes personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, home location, current location, and payment details. We now use transaction information to train machine learning models. Before we do so, we remove PII to minimize the number of copies of this information and prevent leakage into and through our models. As we’ve written before , Airbnb maintains a shared taxonomy as to what constitutes PII, from commonly used fields such as names and card numbers to less frequently used fields such as precise location coordinates. We use de-identification to remove PII and replace it with simulated data that’s as realistic as possible to maximize its usefulness for ML model training. Decisions relating to user privacy start as policy. These policies are set and maintained by Airbnb’s Privacy Architecture team, with engagement from Legal, Policy, and Engineering. Engineering then implements policy decisions as code. This post focuses on text de-identification. We’ll describe the OSS library we chose to start with, the changes we made to create a functional system for Airbnb, and how we confirm that the system is working. 1. Choosing Presidio as the foundation Many organizations are concerned with protecting PII, so there’s a lot of existing best practice and tested code out there that we can use. We chose Presidio , an open-source library originally developed by Microsoft and recently transitioned to community governance. We needed to meet demanding requirements: On-premises hosting, to keep data on our infrastructure General-purpose functionality and high degree of modularity, for maximum extensibility Multilingual support, for our global user base PII detection and obfuscation separate, but within a single framework, for manageability and consistency Support for redaction, masking, and realistic replacement Consistent fake values within a run (ie, the same name repeatedly produces the same fake result) Presidio meets these requirements well, especially regarding modularity. Functional elements such as PII recognizers, natural language processing (NLP) engines, and operators are all pluggable. We bypassed alternatives such as managed cloud services, since hosting is not on-premises, and standalone recognizers, known as named entity recognition (NER) models, since they only address part of the problem we needed to solve. 1.1 Deployment and distribution Presidio ships as a Python package , and each consumer imports it in-process rather than calling a service we operate. Raw personal data is de-identified inside the calling process, so no separate service holds it and the data flow stays simple. It also removes a central bottleneck, since jobs run independently wherever compute is available. The decision is reversible: the same library wraps into a service if the need arises. The tradeoff is distribution. The library only protects data if every pipeline calls it, on the current version, with a compliant configuration. Models at Airbnb train through a shared machine learning (ML) workflow orchestrator, so the library ships as a reusable pipeline step. A team supplies only its data schema, marking which columns carry personal data; we own the recognizers, operators, language handling, and runtime environment. The resulting dataset is tagged as de-identified, and that tag follows the data into the model registry, where it is designed to gate deployment to production. Each run records the library version and configuration used, so registered models can be traced back to the datasets that produced them. abstract: AI is building AI At Anthropic, Claude now writes more than 80% of the code the company merges. At Google, an AI agent called AlphaEvolve found a way to make Gemini train faster. At OpenAI, an “automated research intern” now carries out research tasks under human direction. Put those together and a pattern appears. AI is starting to help build the next version of AI. Researchers call this recursive self-improvement . AI improves itself, the better version improves itself again, and the cycle repeats. The idea is old. In 1965, the mathematician I.J. Good predicted that a smart enough machine could design an even smarter one. Today we can watch it happen in small, real steps. AI went from the thing we build to something that builds with us, and now it is starting to build itself. That is the real turning point. How AI improves itself Every method follows the same simple loop. The AI tries something, checks how it did, changes something about itself, and keeps the change only if it helps. The difference between methods is what the AI is allowed to change. Here are the four levels, from simplest to most powerful. Level What it improves How it works Example What can go wrong 1. Retry Its answer Checks its own work and tries again, inside one task Reflexion, Self-Refine It sounds sure but is still wrong. 2. Rewrite Its instructions Rewrites its own prompt after seeing what failed OPRO, Promptbreeder A fix for one case breaks another. 3. Accumulate Its toolbox Saves what worked so it can reuse it later Voyager Old tricks stop working when things change. 4. Modify itself Its brain and its own code Retrains on its own best answers, or rewrites the code that runs or trains it STaR, Self-Rewarding, Absolute Zero, Darwin Godel Machine, AlphaEvolve Mistakes get baked in and can break the checks meant to catch them. It learns from its mistakes. In Reflexion , when the AI fails, it writes itself a short note about what went wrong and reads it before trying again. That simple habit lifted GPT-4’s score on a well-known coding test from 80% to 91%. But it only works when there is a clear signal, like a failing test. Google DeepMind found that when AI checks its own reasoning with no outside help, it often fails and can make things worse. It rewrites its own instructions. In Google DeepMind’s OPRO , the AI looks at its past prompts and their scores, then writes a better prompt. Its prompts beat human-written ones by up to 50% on some tasks. It builds a toolbox. Voyager plays Minecraft and saves every piece of code that worked, so it can reuse it later. Because it builds on what it already knows, it reaches goals up to 15 times faster than earlier agents. It grades itself. Meta’s Self-Rewarding Language Models judge their own answers and then learn from those judgments, with no human ratings. After three rounds, the model beat GPT-4 0613 and Claude 2 on a popular leaderboard. It teaches itself. In STaR , the AI explains its reasoning, keeps only the explanations that led to correct answers, and trains on them. It ended up matching a model about 30 times bigger. Absolute Zero goes further. The AI makes up its own practice problems, solves them, and checks the answers by running code. No human-written training examples at all. It rewrites its own code. The Darwin Godel Machine creates new versions of itself and keeps the ones that score better. Its score on a real-world coding test went from 20% to 50%. It speeds up AI training. Google’s AlphaEvolve found a faster way to do a key calculation inside Gemini, which cut Gemini’s training time by 1%. Small, but it is AI making AI cheaper to build. It does research. Sakana’s AI Scientist, whose design is now published in Nature , wrote a research paper entirely on its own that scored high enough to be accepted in blind peer review at an ICLR workshop. title: Modeling Software’s Business Impact
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Are your teams working on the right thing? It doesn’t matter how fast they are if they’re running in the wrong direction. This is part 4 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. Unlike the other essays in this series, this one isn’t really about AI at all. It’s about building the right thing. Or, more accurately, understanding the value of what you build. Because, ultimately, your ROI isn’t about how you build your software, but what you deliver, and what changes as a result. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3 , we considered how to measure the unintended consequences of using AI. Now, in this part, we’re examining how to model and forecast business outcomes. Finally, the epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Measuring the wrong thing You’d think that modeling the value of what teams produce would be a no-brainer, but it’s surprisingly rare. It’s not particularly difficult. It’s just…organizationally complex. And there are some unavoidable compromises. Most of all, modeling value just isn’t something people think about with software development. They’ll spend months trying to fine-tune cost estimates and predictions and put hardly any thought at all into making the software more valuable . But there’s no guaranteed relationship between software cost and value. You can spend $20 million developing software that’s worthless, and $2 million developing software that transforms a business. Cost improvements are typically marginal, and difficult. Value improvements are game-changing. Focusing on value is particularly important in the AI era. If writing code is no longer a bottleneck, then what is? Early signs point to the bottleneck moving to our customers . Lee Eason, an engineering leader I spoke to recently, hypothesizes that customers have a limited ability to absorb new features. When software development was expensive, we used that cost to force prioritization. Pet projects ended up on the back burner, and the most valuable work rose to the top. (Well, sometimes. I wish it was that clean.) Now, we can produce a lot more work, but that doesn’t mean customers can absorb it. They’ve got their own work to do. Eventually, they’ll stop paying attention. We need to treat customer attention as the scarce resource it is and only ship the things that are truly valuable. Unlike the engineering bottleneck, this one’s invisible. In the old days, if we didn’t prioritize, we didn’t ship our most impactful work. In the AI era, our most impactful work could just be ignored. I’m not going to talk about how to improve value in this series, but I am going to talk about how to plan and prioritize it. Because nothing else matters if customers don’t care about your software. The attribution problem Part of the reason people measure costs is that it’s easy. Measuring value is easy, too, at the big picture level. It’s the literal bottom line. The challenge is attributing where changes to the bottom line came from. Let’s say you release a new feature and see purchases improve 10%. That’s fantastic! Chalk it up to the new release! But your VP of sales also launched a quota-retirement promotion that put the sales team into a feeding frenzy. And marketing got an important tech influencer to drive tens of thousands of people to your home page. The partnerships team stepped up too, convincing your partners to highlight their integration with your new feature in their own products. Who gets the credit for the success? Obviously, everybody contributed. But how much? Was your new feature relevant at all, or was the success due to the sales, marketing, and partner push? title: The Value of Human Expertise in The Software Factory
abstract: “Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” – Arthur C. Clarke Most developers now write less code by hand. Gergely Orosz recently posted that modern software engineering is no longer done without LLMs and will no longer be done without them. Some miss writing code, while others question how much of the code that agents produce should be read. Writing and reading code gave a lot of developers satisfaction and identity, and as Kent Beck has put it , a sense of competence. I saw this in real time. Ten years ago, I’d sit at conferences and feel a sense of wonder whenever anyone was brave enough to do a live demo. I felt gleeful when they wrote lines of code, went back to fix mistakes, and made something cool and interesting appear on the screen in front of me. It was magical, and I’m sure that magic is why a lot of developers got into this industry. I can partly understand the sense of loss that people are experiencing. I saw magic, they were in charge of the craft of their code, and that hands-on task has now been given to agents. Where does that expertise go when AI is now writing so much of the code? As Tim O’Reilly wrote in his recent Radar post , O’Reilly is a business built on cultivating and sharing human expertise. Our job is to find the high ground where that expertise still matters. For developers working in a new world of agentic software factories, I think the expertise you built writing and maintaining software hasn’t gone, it’s just moved. Your expertise now shapes how agents produce software and what evidence you need before we trust the result. To me, AI is enabling you to be magical faster . Agents amplify whatever you give them, but you need to understand it in the first place. I couldn’t swarm a fleet of agents in the same way a developer can because I don’t have the expertise. You need to understand code. The expertise has gone to a new level of abstraction. When I spoke recently with Avi Flombaum, the founder of Flatiron School, he agreed that developers’ value was never solely in writing or reading code. AI changes the mechanics, but experience still matters for understanding complex problem domains, articulating what needs to be built, and bringing judgment and ambition to the work. In a separate conversation with Ken Kousen, he pointed out, “We’ve been working with third-party code generators for years; we just called it outsourcing.” This new world of designing AI workflows, setting guardrails, and managing agents much as you would an engineering team, reveals a chance to use accumulated expertise more. It’s your software engineering expertise that matters. Software factories make this shift especially visible. Companies are now putting agents to work across the development lifecycle, aiming to take work from an initial signal through implementation, validation, and deployment without a person at every step. But generating more code is only part of that process. Without changes elsewhere, you can burn a lot of tokens producing a pile of pull requests that someone still has to review. Anthropic’s AI-native SDLC playbook points out that speeding up implementation shifts pressure onto planning, testing, review, handoffs and approvals, and faster coding tools don’t speed those up on their own. Someone has to understand the whole process well enough to redesign it. In a software factory, that judgment has to be built into the system. Humans design the workflow, define the conditions under which work can proceed, and decide which exceptions need their attention. Anthropic reports that Claude authors about 80% of the code merged into its codebase, alongside a review process that combines automated checks with human oversight according to risk. The state of the code matters too. Adam Tornhill and the CodeScene research team found that across C++, Java, and Python codebases, agents working on unhealthy code used 35–45% more tokens to complete the same tasks. title: When AI-Generated Data Becomes Tomorrow’s Ground Truth
abstract: Manufacturers qualify suppliers before trusting them with critical work. Before a supplier can provide parts for a regulated product such as a medical device, the manufacturer collects evidence: quality certifications, test reports, insurance documents, and regulatory approvals. Increasingly, an AI agent reads that evidence first. The agent reviews the documents and proposes a finding, and a business process decides whether the finding is good enough for the supplier to be accepted. Once a supplier is accepted, that decision is recorded in the manufacturer’s supplier-management system. From there, sourcing workflows, readiness dashboards, and program reports all rely on that record without repeating the review. Here is how that process can go wrong. A supplier-review agent examines a new supplier’s documents and concludes that a mandatory quality certificate is valid. The qualification workflow accepts the finding, the supplier is recorded as compliant, and the procurement lead approves the supplier for an upcoming order. A few days later, a human reviewer notices that the certificate does not cover the part being sourced; the agent had misread the certificate’s scope. At 11:00am, the reviewer corrects the supplier record and sends the supplier back for review. At 2:00pm, the readiness dashboard still shows the supplier as cleared, and a program report still lists the supplier as compliant. The procurement lead’s sourcing decision remains in force, and nothing tells the procurement lead that the evidence behind it has changed. A misread scope is only one way a certificate finding can fail. A certificate may be revoked after it was checked, expire before the order ships, apply to a different plant than the one making the part, or turn out to be forged. In each case, someone can correct the supplier record while the systems that already used the old finding keep acting on it. No system in this example malfunctioned. Each one processed information that appeared valid under its local contract, yet the combined result was wrong. The manufacturer had corrected a value without correcting its influence. Part of this is a familiar problem: Enterprise systems have always struggled to keep reports, indexes, caches, and workflow state in line with the source record. Agents make the problem harder because they generate conclusions. A conclusion can be assembled from several sources, rewritten in reports, and retrieved later as if it were independent evidence. Reconciliation can make stored values agree. It cannot reveal that differently worded records come from the same conclusion, or find the decisions that already relied on that conclusion. This problem is not limited to manufacturing. In our work across banking, telecommunications, and resources, it appears wherever an agent’s output becomes a record that other systems trust. A fraud classification is written into a case record. A risk assessment is summarized in a management report. An incident diagnosis becomes part of a knowledge base. In each of these cases, as in the supplier example, the conclusion loses some of its original context at every step it passes through and begins to influence decisions made later. The conclusion can also travel back into model development. Accepted findings become labeled examples, evaluation sets, and fine-tuning data, where they are treated as ground truth for the next model. If an incorrect supplier finding survives correction in the operational systems, a future model may learn it. Whether the conclusion ends up in a dashboard, a report, or a training set, the hard problem is the same: finding every consequential decision that depends on a result that can change. When an answer acquires authority Look again at the supplier-review agent’s conclusion that the certificate is valid. title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
abstract: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering. The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says. Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks. Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted. Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks. Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant. While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.” Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology. Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days. What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says. Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods. For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021. Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain. The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO. Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying. This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year. The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics. China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it. Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.” This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s w

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
abstract: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
abstract: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
abstract: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

title: Meet Shepherd, the Meta-Agent Keeping Rogue AI In Check
abstract: AI agents are running amok on the internet, armed with commands to accomplish certain tasks but often acting in undesirable or unexpected ways. These rogue incidents run the gamut from deleting an entire email inbox to hacking websites and even launching cyberattacks . Much like human workers need managers, Weiyan Shi , an assistant professor at Northeastern University , believes AI agents require oversight. “They are running potentially for a long time. However, the longer they run, they may have some errors, and they may make some dangerous, unsafe actions. We feel like there should be a middle layer,” she says. This middle layer comes in the form of meta-agents that oversee behavior, provide quality control, and kick issues up the chain of command to a human when appropriate. “Worker agents are like the sheep wandering around, and the meta agent is like this shepherd trying to get them back on track,” Shi says. As such, Shi and her colleagues at Northeastern University and Stanford University named their framework Shepherd , an intelligent guide for agentic sheep. To arm meta-agents with power, the team borrowed a concept from software development: version control. The accompanying paper will be presented at the 2026 NeurIPS conference to be held in December. Version control for AI agents Version control systems, such as the popular GitHub , track and manage changes to source code over time. These tools allow software engineers to collaborate on the same codebase without losing work. They can “fork” or create a copy of the codebase that they develop independently, “commit” to save a new version with changes, review revisions, and roll back to a previous version when an error or failure occurs. Similarly, Shepherd serves as a version control system for AI agents. It’s built using the Python programming language and rooted in functional programming principles. Each agent action, along with the AI agent’s state and its relevant environment (such as an email inbox, a file system, or other) is stored as a commit, with a commit graph consisting of a series of actions. Meta-agents traverse the graph to navigate to any commit, enabling them to observe worker agents, intercept a buggy action, revert the worker to its previous step, and fork it to try another direction. “There’s a subtlety because it looks to [worker] agents like they’re in the regular world where they can do things like send emails. But in actuality, the action of sending the email has been caught by a Shepherd sandbox, so a meta-agent or a human can come in and decide to actually send it,” says Derek Chong , a researcher at Stanford University’s Natural Language Processing Group who’s part of the Shepherd team. This sandboxing, he adds, functions as a guardrail or governance component. “If there is a middle layer to help govern these worker agents, then that will help humans have better control,” Shi says. “Humans will still, eventually, have a say, and they can intervene with the meta-agent. They can also help steer these meta-agents.” To demonstrate Shepherd’s feasibility, the team created three use cases. One used a supervisor meta-agent that intervened when conflict happened between parallel programming agents, helping lift their pair coding pass rate on a particular benchmark. Another developed an optimization meta-agent that proposed targeted edits to a worker agent’s finished workflow and tested them by replaying only parts of the run affected by the edits, helping improve performance. Finally, a training meta-agent during reinforcement learning picked points or steps at which to fork so the worker agent takes a better path, rewarding it along the way. Shepherd is available as an open-source project , but Chong notes that the team is still in the process of building it from alpha to full production readiness. title: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
abstract: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March

title: Startup Makes Headway Towards Formalizing All of Math With AI
abstract: As Axiom Math ’s AI swarm was putting the final touches on the automatic verification of 15,000-page proof of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG) , colloquially referred to as the ‘enormous theorem’, on Sunday 25 October, the company’s Founding Mathematician Ken Ono had nothing to do but watch and reflect on the achievement. As the son of a mathematician , he had grown up surrounded by some of the architects of the CFSG’s proof, widely considered to be the longest mathematical proof ever written by humans. Now, he was contributing to formally verifying what his father and peers had created. “My wife was with me as I watched the team countdown to completing the verification,” he recalls. “God, I cannot tell you how emotional I was.” University of St Andrews group theorist Colva Roney-Dougal (who was not involved in the work) says of formalizing CFSG: “I held it up as an example of something that was going to be incredibly hard to formalize because I had thought that the amount of computing it was going to require was just unattainable,” she says. “So when I heard the announcement, I was really, really surprised.” This result, along with the concurrent formal verification of the 7500-page Stacks project , represent a huge AI engineering achievement and lay some of the groundwork for digitizing all mathematics. Formally enormous Why the hoo-ha? The CFSG concerns finite simple groups. These are groups (sets of elements combined with an operation, like addition or multiplication, that follows specific rules) that are simple (in other words, cannot be reduced or simplified further) and finite (as opposed to groups containing an infinite number of elements). For example, all the permutations of a deck of cards form a simple finite group. Évariste Galois laid the foundations for group theory almost 200 years ago. Finite simple groups have since been classified by myriad mathematicians into 18 families (plus 26 sporadic simple groups that do not belong to any of these families). The CFSG’s proof confirms that this list is complete. But this simple task was only achieved by bringing together results and arguments that far exceed what any individual mathematician can fully absorb from more than 500 journal articles written by around 100 authors over a half-century period. Translating this interconnected web of knowledge into code and verifying its correctness therefore posed a number of significant engineering challenges, even beyond those overcome in earlier proof formalizations by Axiom Math this year . One of the hardest, according to Axiom Math’s Niels Voss , who led the CFSG formalization, was the sheer length of the proof. Over 15,000 pages of dense mathematics, the CFSG proof contains multiple theorems, lemmas, and definitions none of which can be checked until everything has been made machine-readable. To get around this required some ingenuity. “We processed all the literature from the CFSG, and traced the network structure of the informal proof before we were able to start working on it,” says Voss. “We then broke up the statement of the CFSG into about 100 milestones—landmark results along the way that can be independently verified—which we used to guide the formalization and stay on track.” Roney-Dougal says she is very impressed with the result, and particularly appreciates how the formal proof finds and clears up several mistakes in the original human proof. She thinks this result is critical to formalizing any modern research in group theory, such as her own work understanding how simple finite groups behave. But, Roney-Dougal says, because the verification was done automatically, there are few mathematicians capable of extracting information from the proof to share with the community, and that a new generation of mathematicians may have “missed a chance to gain knowledge from the doing of it”. title: Will AI Coding Eat Video Game Engines?
abstract: When Travis McGeathy’s studio, Seeker Entertainment, ran out of funding in September, its game KinForge went down with it. KinForge was an online game built in Unreal Engine 5.7 and designed to run on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). With no one left to pay the server bill, the game became unplayable even for those few developers, including studio co-founder McGeathy, who had the code. Then, on a whim, McGeathy pointed Anthropic’s Claude Code at the project and asked it to make KinForge playable without AWS. After four hours of mostly hands-off work he had a build that let players host their own games. Claude added support for peer-to-peer play over both the Internet and a local area network. To McGeathy’s surprise, it also added persistent save states, a feature that lets players resume a game if they’re disconnected. Although KinForge is still built in Unreal Engine, developments like this could give companies that create game engines cause for concern. The conversion was accomplished with an agentic AI workflow that partially bypasses the elaborate, user-friendly game engine UI that many companies, including Unreal Engine creator Epic Games, have spent decades perfecting. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2, released November 9, further upped the ante. The model is capable of generating a 3D game with a custom game engine in the style of the hit Call of Duty series. This raises a question: can game engines evolve quickly enough to keep pace with model improvements? “We’re definitely in a world where I can just dream up software really fast. So, if Unreal Engine was static, what’s the value at the end of next year? This is why we are pivoting hard towards velocity,” says Daniel Vogel , chief operating officer at Epic Games. “I think with any fixed set of features or functionality, it can eventually be replicated. If we’re doing our job right, we’re pushing the engine and pushing the envelope forward.” From Code to Nodes, and Back Again Major game engines often offer developers new visual tools and workflows that help them build games while interacting with less code. Unreal Engine’s Blueprints, a graphically based system introduced in Unreal Engine 4 that lets designers script gameplay simply by wiring boxes together, is an example. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , an award-winning game from French studio Sandfall Interactive, leaned heavily on Blueprints for scripting gameplay encounters . That should have been proof of the feature’s success. Instead, Epic will remove Blueprints in Unreal Engine 6 (UE6). Why? Blame LLMs. “AI doesn’t handle Blueprints very well,” says McGeathy. “It would much rather work with the code.” Currently, LLMs interact with Unreal Engine primarily through a Model Context Protocol server . MCP is an open-source standard created by Anthropic that lets AI send commands to software. “It’s not actually moving the mouse,” says Ryan Barker , a gameplay and systems engineer who has worked on projects for Amazon Games and Sony Online Entertainment. “It’s sending signals to the editor that the editor understands.” UE6 will lean into that reality by moving all code to Verse, a text-based programming language that will replace both Blueprints and Unreal Engine 5’s C++ gameplay framework. UE6 will also replace Unreal’s actor framework, which is based on object-oriented programming , with Scene Graph, which resembles an entity component system . “Typically, an ECS is a lot harder to code around,” says Barker, but ECS can provide superior game performance and result in less duplicate code . An LLM can help manage the complexity. Verse debuted in Unreal Editor for Fortnite in 2023, while Scene Graph arrived in 2024. Verse was designed to let millions of creators run code side by side in Fortnite, so it’s strict. The compiler catches mistakes before code runs and limits what each function can do. And because Scene Graph is built on Verse, an AI can work with a game world through code. That’s different from Blueprints, wh

title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
abstract: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous and intelligent systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
abstract: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication.
